sentences.text: It was on the third night that Ren first heard him.
He had stayed up late, sitting on the floor with the radio in front of him.
It was past midnight.
Obaachan had gone to sleep.
He was moving the dial very slowly, listening for interesting stations, when he heard something unusual.
A boy's voice.
Speaking in Japanese, but slowly, and carefully, with a strange formality.
It sounded like a boy his own age.
Ren stopped moving the dial.
The frequency window was on 6.185 megahertz.
The boy was saying, "Hello.
This is Tetsuo.
Can anyone hear me.
Over." There was a pause.
Then the boy said, "I am ten years old.
I live in Kushiro.
Is anyone listening.
Over." There was another pause.
Then the boy tried again.
"Please.
If you hear me.
Please answer.
I have been trying for three months.
Over."
Ren sat very still.
The radio he was listening to did not have a microphone — it could only receive, not transmit.
He could not answer.
He listened.
The boy — Tetsuo — kept talking.
He said his radio call sign, which was a string of letters and numbers.
He said he was doing something called "CQ," which he explained was what radio operators did when they were looking for anyone to talk to.
He said again that he had been trying for three months.
He sounded, Ren thought, a little tired, and a little brave.
After maybe ten minutes, the boy said, "That is all for tonight.
Same time tomorrow, same frequency.
Over and out." And then he was gone.
There was only static.
Ren sat with the headphones on for another few minutes, hoping he would come back.
He did not.
Ren turned off the radio and went to bed.
He lay awake for a long time thinking about it.
In the morning he asked Obaachan about it.
He was trying to be careful.
He asked, "Obaachan, when Ojiichan was a boy, did he have a radio call sign?
For his radio?" Obaachan looked at him for a moment.
"Yes," she said.
"He did.
All of the boys and girls who built their own radios did.
It was how they identified themselves.
Why do you ask." Ren said, "Do you remember what his was?" She thought.
"It was — JA8 something.
JA8AB.
Or JA8AC.
Something like that.
It was a long time ago." Ren nodded.
He did not tell her the rest.
"And what was Ojiichan's name when he was a boy?
His full name." She raised an eyebrow.
"Tetsuo," she said.
"Tetsuo Yamamoto.
Why.
Why do you want to know?" Ren said, "Just curious." And he went outside into the garden and he sat under the persimmon tree for a long time, and he thought about it.
That night Ren listened again.
At exactly the same time.
On exactly the same frequency.
And the same boy was there.
Tetsuo.
Ten years old.
Kushiro.
Which was a city in eastern Hokkaido — not the village where Ren was, but not so far.
The boy did his CQ.
He asked for anyone to answer.
He said he had been trying for three months and now four.
He described the radio he had built himself, out of parts his father had brought home from work.
Ren listened for almost half an hour.
At one point the boy told a small story about school.
He said his teacher had been angry with him because he had been drawing radios instead of doing his math.
He said his father had laughed when he heard about it.
He said he thought the teacher was going to write a note home but the teacher had not.
He said he had felt lucky.
Ren, listening, understood something then.
He was hearing his grandfather.
Ten years old.
In some year in the 1950s.
Speaking into the air of a night that was over long before Ren had been born.
He did not know how it was possible.
He knew about radio waves — that they traveled at the speed of light, that they went out into space.
He wondered if some signals bounced off things very far away and came back many years later.
He wondered if this was one of those.
He also wondered if he was wrong.
If it was some other boy named Tetsuo, in some other place.
If it was a recording someone was broadcasting on purpose.
If he was making it all up in his head.
But he did not think he was making it up.
He thought it was really his grandfather.
And so, that night, before Tetsuo signed off, Ren did something.

He whispered into the empty room, into the radio, into the past — even though he knew the radio could not send anything, and even though he knew nothing could actually go back through time — he whispered, "I hear you, Ojiichan.
I hear you.
It is Ren.
Over and out." And then he took the headphones off, and he turned the radio off, and he went to bed.
